title: Bossing around teams of AI bots is becoming a new job skill — without boss pay
author: Rani Molla
summary: Rani Molla reports in Business Insider that AI is turning individual contributors into de facto managers of agents without the title, training or pay that usually come with management. She profiles engineers, a technical writer, a marketing consultant and a professor who now set expectations for agents, review their output and own the results. A BCG survey of nearly 12,000 employees finds 47% spend more time managing and directing AI than doing the work themselves, while only 36% say they have received adequate upskilling. Visier data shows that of workers whose roles changed because of AI, only 17% have been promoted, and researchers note that managers of people keep the financial advantage. Compensation experts say companies are layering agents onto existing structures and, if they reward the skill at all, will likely do so through bonuses rather than base pay. The piece concludes that workers are being given more responsibility and little else.
points: Supervising agents involves the same core tasks as managing people (setting expectations, delegating, evaluating, demanding revisions, owning the outcome), yet it arrives without title or raise.
The training gap is stubborn: BCG says only 36% feel adequately upskilled, a figure unchanged across its surveys, and generic classroom-style training is not what workers need.
Visier found only 17% of workers whose roles changed due to AI were promoted, and individual contributors already earn about 33% less than team leaders at the same firm.
Workers who craft agent instructions, such as the consultant who builds her judgment into named agents, show that the durable human contribution is defining what good work looks like.
